summary: Intro discovery for MercuryDocs evaluating Redwood hosted vs dedicated vs private. Focus on time-to-first-response for PLG quickstart, free credits, security needs (SSO/KMS/SOC2), and potential benchmark pilot. SE offered a follow-up benchmark session and requested traffic/latency targets.
topics: Hosted vs Dedicated vs Private (VPC/on-prem) tradeoffs
meeting_header: Date: 2025-09-19 | Start: 14:30 PT | Duration: ~58 min | Location: Zoom | Recording: yes
transcript:
[00:00] Jasmine Hart: Hey everyone thanks for taking the time, I'm Jasmine on the AE team at Redwood Inference. Rafael is our solutions engineer. How's everyone doing?
[00:06] Priya Nair: Hi Jasmine, doing well thanks. We have Ben and Tom on the call, Ben will be the main technical lead for this eval.
[00:10] Ben Lui: Yep, hi all.
[00:12] Rafael Ortega: Hey, quick context from our side: we usually lead these discovery calls with a very short checklist — quickstart path, free credits, security constraints, and then figure out if a small dedicated pilot makes sense.
[00:20] Tom Reeves: Sounds good. We're evaluating a hosted-first flow if possible, but want to understand when we need dedicated or private. We have strict data residency regs for some docs.
[00:29] Jasmine Hart: Great. High level — Redwood has a hosted API for fastest time-to-first-response, dedicated reserved pools for predictable throughput, and private VPC/on-prem for regulated workloads. For a PLG/self-serve evaluation we normally give credits so teams can get to first inference in hours.
[00:41] Priya Nair: When you say "hours" what are you referring to? From signup to production-like response? Or just get a toy example?
[00:48] Rafael Ortega: Good distinction. For a developer to get the first token back from the hosted API — meaning a real model call — it's typically under one hour assuming the account is verified and uses the quickstart SDK snippet. To get production-like latency and throughput numbers we'd run a small benchmark which can take a few days depending on model selection and traffic patterns.
[01:05] Ben Lui: And how do the free credits work? Are they tied to specific models or are they generic?
[01:11] Jasmine Hart: Credits are model-agnostic for the hosted API — they cover generation/embedding units. For dedicated or private pilots we usually structure a separate trial contract since we reserve capacity.
[01:20] Priya Nair: We have compliance folks asking about SOC 2 and encryption at rest. Also we use a customer-managed KMS for keys. Do you support that in hosted?
[01:29] Rafael Ortega: Short answer: yes for private and dedicated; for hosted we integrate with customer KMS for enterprise plans — there are a couple of options. I can share the SOC2 pack and a short doc on KMS integrations. There are tradeoffs but we support HSM-backed keys for private deployments.
[01:44] Tom Reeves: What about SSO and RBAC? We don't want open accounts.
[01:48] Jasmine Hart: We support SAML/SSO across tiers for enterprise accounts, and RBAC and audit logs are available; on hosted we can provision organization-level controls for your team.
[01:57] Ben Lui: Ok. From a technical perspective we care about P95 latency under 150ms for short prompts, and costs. Our baseline is 80ms for very short inference on our current internal endpoints.
[02:07] Rafael Ortega: That's a helpful target. For short prompt scenarios P95 ~150ms is achievable on certain hosted model variants — it depends on model architecture and sequence length. We usually recommend a profiling run: give us a representative prompt set and concurrent request profile, we'll run it on hosted and then show cost/latency tradeoffs.
[02:22] Jasmine Hart: Quick question on timeline — are you looking for a self-serve proof-of-concept this quarter?
[02:27] Priya Nair: Ideally yes, we'd like a small evaluation with our prompts within the next 3–4 weeks, then decide if we need dedicated capacity for production Q1.
[02:35] Jasmine Hart: Perfect. Steps we recommend: 1) we'll provision free credits and a quickstart guide; 2) Rafael will request representative load/queries; 3) run an SE-led benchmark session to demonstrate TTFR and cost; 4) recap and recommend hosted vs dedicated sizing.
[02:49] Ben Lui: Sounds sensible. A couple of gotchas we have: some docs contain PII and must not leave the EU, so data residency matters. Also we may need to run an on-prem for a narrow set of workflows.
[02:59] Rafael Ortega: We can do region pinning in hosted for EU regions, and private on-prem is possible for the narrow PII workflows. One note: private/on-prem adds extra ops work and a different licensing model. We'll include those differentiators in the follow-up.
[03:15] Speaker 1: Mm-hmm.
[03:17] Jasmine Hart: Quick cost question — do you have a target run rate for per-month usage during the eval? Even a ballpark helps us size recommendations.
[03:23] Priya Nair: Initially it will be low, maybe 100k tokens/month during eval, but if it looks good we could ramp quickly. We want to know how unit economics change with batching and caching.
[03:33] Rafael Ortega: Batching and KV cache usage can dramatically reduce per-token CPU/GPU utilization. We'll show caching suggestions in the runbook. Also quantization and lower-precision variants give big wins for throughput at slight quality cost.
[03:44] Ben Lui: For the benchmarking session can you simulate our concurrency pattern? We have lots of short, bursty traffic from web clients.
[03:50] Rafael Ortega: Yes, we can model that. Please share your typical concurrent users and request distribution. We'll run load scenarios including warm and cold-cache profiles.
[03:59] Priya Nair: Onboarding friction: our platform security team is strict about third-party access. Will we have to do a lengthy vendor assessment?
[04:06] Jasmine Hart: We get that. We'll provide the security questionnaire answers, SOC2 report, data flow diagrams, and an architecture note for how requests and logs flow in hosted vs private. That usually speeds up vendor review.
[04:20] Tom Reeves: Regarding private deployment, is it a full shipping of Redwood control plane, or do you run a managed control plane in our VPC?
[04:28] Rafael Ortega: For Private we offer a customer-managed control plane option; deployments can be full on-prem or a VPC-hosted stack. For strongly regulated customers we do an air-gapped package as well. We'll detail options and implications in the doc pack.
[04:42] Jasmine Hart: Would you be able to commit to a 60-minute benchmark on Oct 2nd? We can make that SE-led with a rough agenda: validate connectivity + model selection, run representative traffic, review logs and costs, then Q&A.
[04:52] Priya Nair: Oct 2nd works for us.
[04:54] Ben Lui: Yes.
[04:55] Jasmine Hart: Great. I'll send calendar invite and pre-work. Rafael, anything to add on metrics you'll capture?
[05:01] Rafael Ortega: We'll capture P50/P95/P99 latency, tail variance, GPU utilization, tokens/sec, and cost per 1k tokens. We'll also show the impact of batching and cache hits. One nuance: tokenization differences between models can change token counts, so we'll align on tokenizer and prompt templates beforehand.
[05:18] Priya Nair: Do you have any plug-and-play SDK examples for node and python we can drop into our webapp?
[05:24] Jasmine Hart: Yes — we have canonical snippets for Node/Python/Rust and a Next.js example. The quickstart repo includes those. I'll include code links.
[05:31] Ben Lui: About the pricing model: hosted per-token pricing is fine for eval, but if we move to dedicated how do commitments work? Are there burst windows?
[05:40] Jasmine Hart: Dedicated is reserved capacity — you commit to a monthly GPU reservation and get discounted unit costs with burst capacity options for spikes. We'll include a sample commitment schedule in the follow-up.
[05:50] Tom Reeves: What kind of SLAs are typical on Dedicated?
[05:53] Rafael Ortega: We have SLA-backed uptime and latency targets for Dedicated customers; specific SLOs vary by package and region, we'll include the SLA matrix in the pack.
[06:03] Speaker 2: (inaudible)
[06:05] Priya Nair: A practical question — how long does it take to move from hosted eval to dedicated provision? We want minimal downtime.
[06:12] Rafael Ortega: With planning, Dedicated baseline capacity provisioning is usually 2–4 weeks depending on hardware availability and region, less if you're in a cloud region we already have capacity in. The migration can be phased with traffic split and can be near-zero downtime if you use our routing/fallback policies.
[06:26] Ben Lui: Any gotchas around model versions and deterministic outputs? We run QA that expects consistent behavior across versions.
[06:33] Rafael Ortega: Model versioning is first-class; you can pin versions and we support controlled rollouts (canary/A-B). We'll also surface drift alerts if outputs diverge from baseline eval prompts.
[06:45] Jasmine Hart: Ok let's capture next steps quickly — I'll: send quickstart checklist + credits, Rafael: draft benchmark runbook and questions, Priya: send sample prompt set and traffic profile. We'll plan the SE benchmark on 2025-10-02.
[06:58] Tom Reeves: Good. Anything else?
[07:01] Priya Nair: Just ask — is there a sandbox environment that won't consume credits for people experimenting?
[07:06] Jasmine Hart: We can set up a low-cost sandbox with throttled rate limits that uses credits more slowly; it's part of the quickstart plan.
[07:13] Ben Lui: Great.
[07:15] Jasmine Hart: Thanks everyone. We'll follow up with docs and the invite.
[07:18] Speaker 3: Bye.
[07:20] (call ends)

Note: transcription contains minor mis-hearings e.g., "KV cash" in one snippet, occasional overlapping talk and filler words.
